name: Old Norse
confidence_why: 4 independent first-hand descriptions agree (2 state the same rule, 1 refine it); none contradicts.
sweep_summary: Old Norse (oldn1244) is in the catalog as fixed-dominant initial (non-strict), currently decided by a single line in Sweet's 1895 teaching primer. The search of works with stress or accent in the title produced exactly one bibliography item, van Leyden 2004 (LOT 92, Leiden thesis on Orkney and Shetland prosody). I downloaded the open LOT full text (HTTP 200, saved with extracted text under and read it: it is an experimental study of vowel/consonant duration and intonation (pitch-peak alignment) in present-day Orkney and Shetland Scots dialects; Norn/Old Norse figures only as the substratum, 'Old Norse' never occurs, and nothing is said about Old Norse word-stress placement. Glottolog itself flags the Old Norse link as a computational keyword assignment from 'shetland'. Relevance: another language or variety; silent on the catalog; acquisition priority none. No other stress/accent/prosody-titled work exists for this language in this search of works with stress in the title. For the best new statement I re-read the sources already held in our files from an earlier compilation: Noreen 1923 sec. 51 (root-initial main stress with listed for-/of-/tor- and -ing/-ung alternates), Barnes 2008 p. 8 ('Stress was in principle always on the first syllable'), and Goering 2023 sec. 12.4 (moraic trochees left-to-right, leftmost foot primary; end-rule left). All confirm the initial-dominant, non-strict coding; Noreen's reference grammar (with Barnes 2008 as the plain English statement) should supersede Sweet 1895 as the deciding source, as our earlier reading record already proposed. no reclassification. A was listing all six copies we hold with citations and URLs.

new_statements.quote: 1. Der hauptton ruht der regel nach: a) In zusammengesetzten Wörtern auf der Wurzelsilbe des ersten gliedes. Jedoch gibt es nicht wenige Wörter, bei denen die Wurzelsilbe des letzten gliedes wenigstens alternativ den hauptton trägt. Solche sind die meisten auf for- (fyr-) 'ver-', of- 'allzu' und tor- 'schwer' [...] b) In einfachen Wörtern auf der Wurzelsilbe. Jedoch dürfte in einzelnen fällen die ableitungssilbe, wenigstens alternativ, haupttonig gewesen sein; so besonders in vielen mit -ing- und -ung- abgeleiteten Wörtern, z. b. þrenning dreieinigkeit, minning erinnerung
new_statements.translation: 1. The main stress rests as a rule: a) in compound words on the root syllable of the first member. However, there are not a few words in which the root syllable of the last member carries the main stress, at least as an alternative. Such are most of those in for- (fyr-) 'ver-', of- 'too', and tor- 'hard to' [...] b) in simplex words on the root syllable. However, in individual cases the derivational syllable may have been main-stressed, at least alternatively; especially in many words derived with -ing- and -ung-, e.g. þrenning 'trinity', minning 'remembrance'.
new_statements.citation: Noreen, Adolf. 1923. Altisländische und altnorwegische Grammatik (Laut- und Flexionslehre) unter Berücksichtigung des Urnordischen. 4. Aufl. Halle: Max Niemeyer. sec. 51 'Betonung', pp. 46-47 (archive.org altislndischeu00noreuoft scanned text, lines 3348-3407).
new_statements.reading: Primary stress is root-initial: on the root syllable of a simplex and on the root of the first member of a compound; the listed exceptions (for-/of-/tor- prefixed compounds and some -ing/-ung derivatives, where the later root/suffix could take main stress at least alternatively; clitics unstressed) make the initial pattern dominant but not exceptionless. This matches the catalog's fixed-dominant, not in the strict set coding. The same pattern is stated in plain English by Barnes 2008 (NION I, sec. 2.1, p. 8, file line 586): 'Stress was in principle always on the first syllable', and formalised by Goering 2023 sec. 12.4 pp. 213-214 (principle 9: 'The leftmost foot carries the primary word stress (end-rule left)').

new_statements.translation: As regards the expiratory accent, a syllable could be main-stressed, strongly secondary-stressed, weakly secondary-stressed or unstressed. [...] 1. The main stress rests as a rule: a) In compound words on the root syllable of the first member. However, there are not a few words in which the root syllable of the last member carries the main stress, at least alternatively. Such are most of those in for- (fyr-) 'ver-', of- 'too', and tor- 'hard', e.g. forboþ 'prohibition', ofmiok 'too much', torkenna 'to make unrecognisable' [...] b) In simple words on the root syllable. However, in individual cases the derivational syllable may have been main-stressed, at least alternatively; so especially in many words derived with -ing- and -ung-

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (initial stress = initial stress) and identical to the existing statement, which already quotes this section of this edition. The reread confirms the existing quote verbatim and adds the four-grade stress hierarchy, the secondary-stress rules of points 2-3, the clitic rule of point 4, and Noreen's caveat that Old West Norse accentuation is only partly established and presumed to match earliest Old Swedish.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Main (expiratory) stress falls on the root syllable: in simplex words on the root, in compounds on the root of the first member. Since Old Norse roots are word-initial (prefixes are rare and the listed prefixed cases are the exceptions), this is word-initial stress. Noreen opens the section by saying that Old West Norse accentuation is still little investigated in detail and is presumed to match earliest Old Swedish (p. 46). § 32 (p. 41) says stress and pitch are not marked in the grammar; § 33 Anm. 2 says manuscripts sometimes mark the position of main stress with the accent sign.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Four grades: main stress, strong secondary, weak secondary, unstressed (p. 46). Strong secondary stress (2, pp. 47-48): on the root syllable of the non-main-stressed member of a compound (kirkiogarþr), but the last member is weak in suffixed-article forms (barnet) and in words no longer felt as compounds (Sigurþr, tottogo); in simplex words on many derivational syllables -and, -ind, -und, -ing, -ung, -ern, -ug, -ul, -ur (eigande, vikingr, lausung), dialectally weak. Weak secondary stress (3, p. 48) falls as a rule on the syllable immediately following the main-stressed syllable of a simplex (tunga, kallaþe); absent in most disyllabic comparatives (stœrre, yngre, betre) and in some words like nio, tio. Anm. 1: after a short main-stressed syllable the following secondary stress was earlier, and still in some Old Norwegian dialects, somewhat stronger ('halbstark'), e.g. gata, talaþe.
new_statements.exceptions: Compounds where the last member carries main stress at least alternatively: most in for-/fyr-, of-, tor-; many in á-, iafn-, ú- (beside main-stressed ó-), e.g. ásiöna, iafnsterkr, úhreinn; and a number of individual words with a monosyllabic first member, especially where both members have a long vowel (miskunn, fátœkr, gáleyse, framfarenn, hórdómr, rettlátr, hugskot, nálœgr, the numerals in -tán such as sextán). Doublets reflect alternative stress (lík(h)amr : likamr, fóst(r)syster : fósyster, Grik(k)land : Girkland, bryllaup : brullaup). Simplex words: some -ing-/-ung- derivatives with main stress on the suffix (þrenning, minning, kenning, teningr beside þrenneng etc.). Unstressed: root syllables of proclitic and enclitic words (eþa, meþan, ekke beside stressed ekke, þikkia beside stressed þykkia) (4, p. 48).
new_statements.identity_note: Noreen 1923 covers Old Icelandic and Old Norwegian (Old West Norse) with reference to Proto-Norse; the stress section says Old West Norse accentuation is presumed to agree with the earliest Old Swedish. Dialect remarks: Old Norwegian more often úrœinn than órœinn (p. 47); the 'halbstark' secondary stress after a short main-stressed syllable survives especially in certain Old Norwegian dialects (Anm. 1, p. 48); strong secondary stress on derivational syllables can be weak dialectally (p. 48).

tone_statements.citation: Sólveig Hilmarsdóttir & Haukur Þorgeirsson. 2025. From the Aeneid to Accent Theory: The Application of Classical Learning in the Medieval Icelandic Third Grammatical Treatise. International Journal of the Classical Tradition 32(4): 383-410.
tone_statements.quote: The evidence showing that Old Norse was a pitch-accent language is extensive. Most modern Swedish and Norwegian dialects have a pitch contour distinction that etymologically must be traced to processes active during the Old Norse or Proto-Norse periods. ... The forms bǽnúm (‘prayers’, dat. pl., accent 2, with two pitch peaks) and bæ̂num (‘farm’, dat. sg. definite form, accent 1, with one pitch peak) are a minimal pair distinguished only by their pitch contours—something which Latin did not have but which Greek did.
tone_statements.summary: Holds Old Norse was a pitch accent language with a two-way word accent (accent 1 vs 2, one vs two pitch peaks), read from the treatise's accent marks; cites Riad 1998 and Árnason & Þorgeirsson 2017.

tone_statements.citation: Haukur Þorgeirsson. 2013. Hljóðkerfi og bragkerfi: Stoðhljóð, tónkvæði og önnur úrlausnarefni í íslenskri bragsögu ásamt útgáfu á Rímum af Ormari Fraðmarssyni. Doktorsritgerð (PhD dissertation), Háskóli Íslands, Hugvísindastofnun, Reykjavík.
tone_statements.quote: Kenning um aðgreinandi tónkvæði: Í máli skáldanna var framburðarmunur á orðum með fornar /r/-endingar og fornar /ur/-endingar svo að pör eins og fögr-sögur eða góðr-bróður mynduðu ekki fullkomið rím í framburði. Munurinn fólst í einhvers konar yfirsneiðarlegum þætti sem á sér ættingja í norsk-sænsku tónkvæði og danskri raddglufuþrengingu. Þannig myndu orðmyndir eins og fögur og góður hafa framburð í ætt við fyrra tónkvæði en orðmyndir eins og sögur og bróður framburð í ætt við seinna tónkvæði. Á 16. öld hverfur aðgreinandi tónkvæði úr málinu ...
tone_statements.translation: Theory of distinctive tonal accent: In the poets' language there was a pronunciation difference between words with old /r/ endings and old /ur/ endings, so that pairs like fögr-sögur or góðr-bróður did not form a perfect rhyme in pronunciation. The difference consisted in some kind of suprasegmental feature related to the Norwegian-Swedish tonal accent and the Danish stød. Thus forms like fögur and góður would have a pronunciation akin to accent 1 but forms like sögur and bróður a pronunciation akin to accent 2. In the 16th century the distinctive tonal accent disappears from the language ...
tone_statements.locator: sec. 9.5 'Tónkvæði sem útskýring á stoðhljóðsvandamálinu', p. 218; cf. 9.3 p. 217 ('Ólafur Þórðarson segir berum orðum að íslenska hafi haft aðgreinandi tónkvæði') and 9.12 pp. 231-232
tone_statements.summary: Argues Old and pre-Reformation Icelandic had a Scandinavian-type accent 1/2 contrast, lost in the 16th c; evidence: 13th-c. bænum pair (after Myrvoll & Skomedal) and rhyme; 60+ marked forms in ch. 9.

tone_statements.citation: Myrvoll, Klaus Johan & Trygve Skomedal. 2010. Tonelagsskilnad i islendsk i Tridje grammatiske avhandling. Maal og Minne 102(1): 68-97. Oslo: Novus. (OJS metadata lists the authors as Skomedal, Trygve; Myrvoll, Klaus Johan; the printed byline is 'Av Klaus Johan Myrvoll og Trygve Skomedal'.)
tone_statements.quote: I barbarismane er det derimot ein forvitneleg ny analyse av tvostavingsordet Mána som kann tyda på at Óláfr hev freista å gjeva att ein tonegang lik den me finn i ord med tvostavings tonelag i norske målføre, og ikkje minst gjev umdømingi hans av ordformi bænum i det tolvte verset sterke prov for at det hev funnest tonelagsskilnad i islendsk. [...] um ein ikkje vil meina at det Óláfr skriv i dette stykket, berre er lærde hugskot, tvingar den slutningi seg fram at gamalislendsk hev havt tonelagsskilnad til liks med dei fastlandsnordiske måli.
tone_statements.translation: In the barbarismi, on the other hand, there is an interesting new analysis of the disyllabic word Mána which may indicate that Óláfr tried to render a pitch contour like the one we find in words with disyllabic tone accent (accent 2) in Norwegian dialects, and not least his judgement of the word form bænum in the twelfth verse gives strong proof that a tone-accent distinction existed in Icelandic. [...] unless one wants to hold that what Óláfr writes in this passage is mere learned fancy, the conclusion forces itself that Old Icelandic had a tone-accent distinction just like the Mainland Nordic languages.
tone_statements.locator: p. 94, section 'Slutning' (conclusion); cf. abstract p. 68 and 'Uppsummering' p. 93
tone_statements.n_tones: 2 word accents (tonem 1 'einstavings tonelag' vs tonem 2 'tvostavings tonelag')…

tone_statements.citation: Kock, Axel. 1891. Fornnordiska kvantitets- och akcentfrågor. Arkiv för nordisk filologi 7: 334-377.
tone_statements.quote: 1) Det samnordiska språket använde akc. 1 i ord, som förlorat en på urnordisk ståndpunkt omedelbart efter rotstavelsen följande vokal, vare sig att orden i det samnordiska språket voro en- eller flerstaviga, enkla eller sammansatta. ... Äkc. 2 användes av ord, livilka bevarat den (med en biakcent uttalade) ändelaevokal, som i urnordisk tid omedelbart efterföljde rotstavelsen, t. ex. steinar ... Denna tväspetsiga fortis var måhända av delvis annan art än den tvåspetsiga fortis på stetnn (liksom ordens musikaliska akcentuering var olika).
tone_statements.translation: 1) The Common Norse language used acc. 1 in words that had lost a vowel which, at the Proto-Norse stage, immediately followed the root syllable, whether in Common Norse the words were mono- or polysyllabic, simple or compound. ... Acc. 2 was used by words which preserved the ending vowel (pronounced with a secondary accent) that in Proto-Norse times immediately followed the root syllable, e.g. steinar ... This two-peaked fortis was perhaps of a partly different kind from the two-peaked fortis on steinn (just as the musical accentuation of the words was different).
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Two word accents (acc.1 = acute, acc.2 = circumflex) reconstructed for Common Old Norse, each expiratory + musical, on root-stressed words; argued from Sw/No/Da reflexes; 20+ forms.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: The record codes Old Norse as fixed-dominant initial (non-strict) on a single line from Sweet's 1895 teaching primer; no source file was held and the grade field is empty. I downloaded the Gutenberg text and confirmed the quote verbatim at sec. 20. I then downloaded three stronger open sources: Barnes 2008 (p. 8: 'Stress was in principle always on the first syllable'), Noreen 1923 sec. 51 (main stress on the root syllable of simplexes and of the first member of compounds, with listed exceptions: for-/of-/tor- prefixed compounds and some -ing/-ung derivatives may carry main stress later in the word; clitics unstressed), and Goering 2023 sec. 12.4 (moraic trochees left-to-right, leftmost foot takes primary stress). All confirm root-initial primary stress; Noreen's exceptions justify not in the strict set rather than any reclassify. The classification stands; the action is to re-cite the record to Barnes 2008 p. 8 +

sources.quote: Norse prosody: '1. Form moraic trochees from left to right. 2. Root syllables of lexical items must be footed. ... 8. The heads of (non-extrametrical) feet are stressed. 9. The leftmost foot carries the primary word stress (end-rule left).' I.e. primary stress root-initial; weight matters only for footing/secondary stress.
sources.note: Only recent phonology monograph on Norse word prosody (metrical evidence); gives the foot-based analysis (moraic trochees L-to-R, end-rule left) behind 'initial stress' and could fill the record's empty 'heavy'/secondary-stress fields.

Þannig myndu orðmyndir eins og fögur og góður hafa framburð í ætt við fyrra tónkvæði en orðmyndir eins og sögur og bróður framburð í ætt við seinna tónkvæði. tone.translation: Theory of distinctive tonal accent: In the poets' language there was a pronunciation difference between words with old /r/ endings and old /ur/ endings, so that pairs like fögr-sögur or góðr-bróður did not form a perfect rhyme in pronunciation. The difference consisted in some kind of suprasegmental feature related to the Norwegian-Swedish tonal accent and the Danish stød. Thus forms like fögur and góður would have a pronunciation akin to accent 1 but forms like sögur and bróður a pronunciation akin to accent 2. In the 16th century the distinctive tonal accent disappears from the language ...

tone.translation: In the barbarismi, on the other hand, there is an interesting new analysis of the disyllabic word Mána which may indicate that Óláfr tried to render a pitch contour like the one we find in words with disyllabic tone accent (accent 2) in Norwegian dialects, and not least his judgement of the word form bænum in the twelfth verse gives strong proof that a tone-accent distinction existed in Icelandic. tone.translation: 1) The Common Norse language used acc. 1 in words that had lost a vowel which, at the Proto-Norse stage, immediately followed the root syllable, whether in Common Norse the words were mono- or polysyllabic, simple or compound. ... Acc. 2 was used by words which preserved the ending vowel (pronounced with a secondary accent) that in Proto-Norse times immediately followed the root syllable, e.g. steinar ... This two-peaked fortis was perhaps of a partly different kind from the two-peaked fortis on steinn (just as the musical accentuation of the words was different).

tone.quote: So, did old or Old Norse/Icelandic have word accents? This is not our interpretation; we do not assume that Old Icelandic had a systematic or lexicalised tonal distinction of the Scandinavian type, but we have shown that utterances could show minimal distinctions based on the interplay between word phonology and intonation, which might have been lexicalised and become distinctive. ... this may be associated with a final fall at the end of the stems of original monosyllables, which had become disyllabic.

tone.quote: The ‘peak delay’ scenario takes as its starting point a different observation, namely that the distribution of accent 1 and accent 2 is largely predictable from the number of syllables in the word at the Old Scandinavian stage. In this scenario, accent 1 on dom ‘judgement’ is attributable to the fact that it goes back to an Old Scandinavian monosyllabic form, like Old Icelandic dómr, whereas the accent 2 on döma is due to the disyllabic shape of a form like Old Icelandic dæma. In this scenario, the rise of a distinctive tonal accent is connected ... with later disruptions in syllable count.

tone.quote: I believe that the Scandinavian languages primarily had only stød ~ no stød but that later the opposition acc. 1 ~ acc. 2 sprang up and overlay the original units. ... These are then the main ideas of our reconstruction. 1) The Old Scandinavian languages were mora-counting and the tool of mora-counting in them was the stød. ... since the Danish stød in monosyllables signifies the existence of two moras (“length”), all vowels which are traditionally reconstructed as long must have had stød.
